claims.text: The proposed initial material is a coarse- or moderately-grained, single-phase CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy.
Sliding wear can form an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer in coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi.
Dynamic amorphization is responsible for the wear-induced near-surface refinement.
The wear-induced ultra-nanocrystalline layer promotes rapid passivation under tribo-corrosion conditions.
The wear-induced layer simultaneously moderates mechanical wear and corrosion.
Dynamic surface refinement is the single mediator coupling the wear and corrosion responses.
Mechanically induced grain refinement increases surface area and the number of reactive sites.
The additional surface area and reactive sites accelerate protective oxide-film formation.
The resulting passivation film slows corrosion.
The evolved ultra-nanocrystalline microstructure changes the wear response and is associated with low friction and wear.
Coupling between refinement, passivation, and wear produces total degradation below that expected if wear and corrosion acted independently.
Relative to a specimen without significant wear-induced refinement, tribo-corrosion produces lower or controlled total degradation.
Accelerated passivation reduces the corrosion component of degradation.
CoCrFeMnNi exhibits low friction and remarkably low wear in an inert environment.
An inert environment mitigates oxidation and formation of mixed metal-oxide films.
The proposed mechanism should hold when the environment supports rapid formation of a stable passive oxide.
The mechanism should weaken or fail in highly chloride-rich electrolytes because passivation is inhibited.
The mechanism should weaken or fail when sliding does not induce sufficient dynamic amorphization.
The corrosion rate is predicted to decrease relative to the inert baseline under otherwise similar wear conditions.

contradictions.description: The inert baseline is defined as having minimal corrosion, yet the falsification rule requires the corrosion rate in the corrosive, passivating environment to be lower than that inert baseline. This is inconsistent with both the baseline definition and the stated comparison to a specimen without refinement.

The predicted outcome invokes a baseline without significant wear-induced refinement, whereas the actual inert baseline is tied to the cited study in which low wear is explicitly linked to formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer.

Failure to generate sufficient dynamic amorphization is treated as a boundary where the mechanism is not expected to operate, but the falsification rule also treats absence of the refined layer as falsifying the mechanism.

The mediator is described as both ultra-nanocrystalline and dynamically amorphized without specifying whether these are sequential, coexisting, or alternative states; a fully amorphous layer and an ultra-nanocrystalline layer are structurally distinct.
